object memory · view-direction read-out

Which side of it am I looking at?

Give every object its own turntable in memory. Walk round a chair, store a handful of snapshots each tagged with the angle you took it from — and later a fresh photo tells you which side you are standing on. No pose input. Appearance alone.

This page is the instrument. Pick an object, scrub the orbit, watch it work or fail. It fails in two ways, and they need opposite fixes.

what it does well
  • The circle is a real circle — a full lap returns the identical code, to 1e-16. Rotating the object is one multiply.
  • Reading it is one FFT, and you get the whole answer: how likely every angle is, not just a best guess.
  • Track it over time and the answer settles — 17° → 6°.
where it breaks
  • It cannot guess sides you never looked at. Leave a 30° hole and the error inside it is ~27°.
  • A cube looks the same from four sides. That is not a mistake — there are genuinely four right answers.
  • Sharpening the code makes it worse, not better. Reach beats precision when views are sparse.
added since — eight experiments later

The four sections above this line were measured at ssp_dim=151, max_harmonic=8. One of those two numbers was wrong, and finding out took eight experiments, five of which refuted their own prediction. The four sections below carry what came out:

  • Watch it turn — the orbit as a film, with optical flow beside it, and the memory’s belief updating frame by frame.
  • Occlusion costs 3°, the gap costs 8° — where the errors actually live. Not where you would guess.
  • One setting was wrong — max_harmonic is a capacity knob, not a resolution knob, and 8 was the wrong side of the optimum.
  • The scoreboard — every prediction, and what happened to it.
Where these numbers come from

Objects I rendered, described with HOG — not a camera, not DINOv2, not a robot. The page shows you a mechanism; please don't quote the degrees as a measurement of anything real. The algebra underneath is a different matter: the circle closing exactly, and the one-FFT read-out matching a brute-force scan, are checked to 1e-16 and hold regardless of the data.

Every viewpoint at once

Each row is one photo you showed the memory. Reading across that row: how strongly it believes the photo was taken from each direction — bright means “probably here”. One clean bright line running diagonally means it gets the angle right every time. Several parallel lines mean the object looks the same from several sides, so the question genuinely has more than one answer. Try L_block, then cube.

It fails in two different ways

Lumping both into one error number hides the important distinction: one is a property of the object that no amount of extra data will fix, the other is a coverage problem that more stored sides solves directly.

aliasing

The likelihood has several equal peaks

The object genuinely looks the same from more than one side, so the peak height carries no information about which one you are at. The estimator is not wrong — the question has more than one right answer. Watch the cube in the dial above: four-fold symmetry, four peaks.

— median error at aliased azimuths (— of 216)
single peak

One peak, and the error is the distance to it

Where the likelihood is unimodal, what remains is how far the nearest stored side is. The code interpolates between sides it holds and does not extrapolate past them, so error here is a coverage number, not a representational one.

— median error at unimodal azimuths (— of 216)

Both figures are computed in the page from the same data driving the dial, so they cannot drift from what you see above. A peak counts as competing when it reaches 80% of the maximum and sits more than two kernel widths away.

It cannot teleport — adding continuity

Decoded frame by frame, the estimate jumps 50°, 100°, 180° between consecutive crops. A camera orbiting an object cannot do that, and every one of those jumps is the decoder throwing away the strongest prior it has: you were near here a moment ago. Feeding the likelihood into a Bayes filter on the circle fixes it, and both steps of the filter are native to this representation.

the filter, in the same algebra
stepon the circlein harmonics
predictshift the belief by the odometry step, then blur itB_k ← B_k · e−ikΔ · e−σ²k²/2
updatemultiply by the appearance likelihoodb ← b · softmaxβ(L)

The first factor in the predict step is binding by S_view(Δ) — the same operation as orbit(). The second is per-harmonic damping. Nothing outside the representation was needed. This is the view-circle twin of the position filter in RESULTS_SO_FAR.md finding 6.

estimated direction over one full orbit 72 frames · 5° apart
dashed grey is the truth · click to isolate a trace

Where the green trace seems missing, it is underneath the teal one. For five of the six objects the anchor changes almost nothing — the filter finds the right branch on its own, and free and anchored agree to about a degree. Switch off free start to confirm it. The exception is cube, where they run 88° apart for most of the orbit: that is the whole difference between four branches and one. Vertical breaks in the orange trace are the impossible jumps.

Continuity fixes the coverage failure

read-outmedian errorlargest jumpimpossible jumps
per frame, no memory17.0°180°89 / 426
+ Bayes filter, free start6.0°175°25 / 426
+ one known starting direction4.0°42°11 / 426

A jump counts as impossible above 15° — three times the true 5° step. The filter coasts across the held-out arcs on prediction instead of guessing, which is where most of the error went.

It does not fix aliasing — but an anchor does

cubemedian errorlargest jumpimpossible
per frame83.0°180°27
+ filter, free start87.0°175°10
+ known start2.0°11°0

Four equal branches give the filter nothing to choose between, so tracking alone wanders. But continuity turns a per-frame ambiguity into a single global one: fix the branch once, at the start, and it stays fixed. Symmetry costs one piece of information for the whole trajectory, not one per frame.

Two different things are called anisotropy

One of them is the encoder’s fault and one of them is not, and they need opposite responses. All three numbers below come from the crops alone — no object file, no split, no decode.

removable

Between-object

The leading principal directions say which object this is — PC0 carries 83.8% between-object variance, PC1 70.5%. These are what the conditioning recipe deletes.

not the encoder

Across-view

Seven views spanning 30° of orbit occupy about 3.8 effective dimensions out of 1764 — and that number does not move when you condition. It is what walking a continuous trajectory produces, for any encoder. The same thing as scene redundancy in a video.

They are linked, but backwards from the obvious guess

An object’s identity does not change as you walk around it. So the identity-carrying directions are constant along the orbit, and sit as a DC pedestal on the appearance autocorrelation, lifting every lag equally. Deleting them does not create angular information — it unmasks what was already there.

appearance half-widthindependent views per orbitlocal rank
raw HOG, centred28°2.83.8
top 2 PCs dropped18°6.23.8
view kernel, for comparison16°——

Conditioning buys contrast, not information. Half-width nearly halves and effective sample size more than doubles, while the intrinsic local dimensionality does not move at all.

Aliasing is visible in the descriptor, before any map exists

objectalias peakat circular lagmeasured error
cube0.91090°90.5°
mug0.58135°29.5°
pot0.57835°27.5°
console0.327180°24.0°
chair0.30090°36.5°
L_block0.27335°25.0°

The cube stands alone at 0.910, peaking exactly at its 90° symmetry. One autocorrelation per object tells you which instances will be unlocalisable and at what offset — which is precisely the information the continuity filter needs an anchor for.

It has to be circular distance. On a 72-view ring, a lag of 355° is the adjacent frame. Scanning linear lag makes five of six objects report their own neighbour as an alias. That bug was in the first version of this analysis and inverted the ranking.

The pedestal law

The two anisotropies are one mechanism, and it has an exact form. Split each crop embedding into a global mean, a part that stays constant as you walk around the object — its identity — and a part that actually varies with viewpoint.

zo(φ) = μ + ao + vo(φ),    ⟨vo(φ)⟩φ = 0

λo = ‖ao‖² / ( ‖ao‖² + ⟨‖vo(φ)‖²⟩ )   — the identity fraction

Because ⟨v⟩ = 0 the cross terms vanish on average, and the autocorrelation of the normalised key separates into an affine contrast map with no free parameters:

ρo(Δ) = λo + (1 − λo) · ro(Δ)

λ is measured, not fitted. Tested pointwise over every lag on all six objects: RMS 0.002–0.016, worst single deviation 0.032.

measured ρ against the model, and what λ does to it drag λ to see the pedestal lift and compress the curve
0°angular lag Δ180°
λ 0.37
r(Δ) — view-varying part alone ρ(Δ) — measured key λ + (1−λ)r — the model

Three things that looked separate are corollaries of it

quantitywhat the pedestal does to it
alias marginρ(0) − ρ(Δ) = (1−λ)(1 − r(Δ)). Every contrast is scaled down. The pot at λ = 0.746 keeps a quarter of its available margin even if its view signal were perfect.
half-widthρ reaches ½ where r reaches (½−λ)/(1−λ) < ½ — at a larger lag. The pedestal inflates the measured correlation length. This is the 28° → 18°.
effective sample sizeτ = 1 + 2mλ + 2(1−λ)Σrk. That middle term grows with the summation window and has nothing to do with view correlation, so Neff on unconditioned keys is not well defined — it depends on how many lags you chose to sum.

So removing the identity component is a contrast stretch of gain 1/(1−λ). It reorders nothing and creates no information — but it rescales the half-width, the alias margin and the effective sample size, and all three are used to size design decisions. That is the precise sense in which conditioning buys contrast rather than information.

A conjecture this refuted

If the appearance width caps resolution, then sharpening the view kernel past it should buy nothing. Swept over max_harmonic, five random projections each, at a 30° held-out gap:

kernel half-widthmedian error
34°25.6° ± 1.7
28°27.7° ± 5.6
20°30.1° ± 1.9
16°30.4° ± 2.7
11°29.3° ± 2.6
8°33.3° ± 1.5
6°33.0° ± 4.7

Spread 7.7° against a seed sd of 2.9° — real at 2.6×, but with the opposite sign. Error rises as the kernel sharpens. At sparse coverage the binding constraint is not resolution but reach: a broad kernel spans the held-out arc, a sharp one falls into it. Match the kernel to the stored-view spacing, not to the appearance width — and never sharpen past coverage, because the resolution gained cannot be used and the reach lost is immediate.

The DINOv2 row is missing, and stays missing

Everything on this page runs on HOG. The obvious next column is DINOv2, and it is not here because this environment's egress policy refuses huggingface.co, dl.fbaipublicfiles.com and download.pytorch.org — all three return 403 before TLS. There is no honest way to fill that column from here, so it is left empty rather than substituted.

The wiring exists and is one flag on a machine that can reach the weights:

python experiments/run_view_localisation.py --encoder dinov2 --plot

What to expect to change: DINOv2's spectrum is far flatter than HOG's — 49 of 256 directions carry half the variance against about 3 here — so the latent-conditioning depth will not transfer. The two failure modes should, since aliasing is a property of the object and coverage is a property of the orbit, and neither depends on the encoder. High-norm outlier patch tokens are the one DINOv2-specific hazard, and the --encoder dinov2 path already drops tokens above twice the median norm before pooling.

A hypothesis this page refutes

The obvious explanation was that localisation fails where appearance stops changing with angle — a flat stretch of the orbit gives nothing to key on. It is wrong. The correlation between local appearance rate |dc/dφ| and error is positive (ρ = +0.38): appearance changing faster goes with worse localisation, the opposite of the prediction.

Correction — an earlier version of this page quoted “n = 216, p = 7.6e-9”

That n counted frames. Consecutive views on an orbit are strongly correlated, so they are not independent samples: integrating the appearance autocorrelation gives about 6 independent views per 72-frame orbit, making the effective n nearer 19 than 216. The p-value was therefore meaningless and has been withdrawn. The sign and the ranking below stand — ρ is positive under every leave-one-object-out exclusion, and the aliasing split is a difference between two large groups rather than a correlation. Any interval computed by resampling frames needs a hierarchical bootstrap over objects, arcs and seeds instead.

Applying the breadth check from RESULTS_SO_FAR.md — does the effect survive removing its strongest object? — it does survive, but weakly, and the sign never flips:

excluded objectρ (rate vs error)n
none — all objects+0.380216
chair+0.408180
mug+0.417180
cube+0.220180
L_block+0.412180
pot+0.380180
console+0.415180

The cube halves it, which is the tell: the cube has both the fastest appearance change (sharp faces flipping) and the worst error (it aliases). Rate was a proxy for symmetry, not a cause. Restricted to unimodal azimuths only, ρ falls to +0.202 and the gradient is nearly flat — median error 21.8° → 24.5° → 26.8° across the full range of appearance rate. Peak multiplicity explains the failures; appearance rate barely does.

It interpolates. It does not extrapolate.

Widening the held-out arc moves the nearest kept side further away. Error inside the gap tracks that distance almost linearly up to chance, while the control — the same object file read at sides it kept — never moves. The file is not degraded by the harder split; the missing viewpoints simply are not recoverable.

held-out arcnearest kept sidein-gap medianwithin 15°control
interleaved (the original, leaky split)5.0°8.0°0.667.0°
10°5.0°10.8°0.588.0°
20°7.5°21.2°0.365.0°
30° (shown in the dial)10.0°27.5°0.186.0°
45°15.0°36.8°0.087.5°
60°17.5°59.0°0.067.0°
90°25.0°79.2°0.046.0°

Chance is 90°. A constant predictor also scores 90°. The interleaved row is the split the earlier draft used, and it overstated accuracy by roughly 3×.

What each failure asks for

for aliasing

Break the symmetry or report the ambiguity

  • More stored sides do nothing — the peaks stay equal.
  • Return the whole likelihood, not the argmax. ViewLocalisation.margin already measures the gap to the runner-up peak, and it is small exactly here.
  • Fuse with odometry rather than trusting the peak; a flat multi-peak likelihood is still informative as a likelihood.
  • Break the tie with a cue the pooled descriptor discards — a part at a known surface location is the natural candidate.
for coverage

Store sides at the kernel's spacing

  • To localise better than 15°, sides must sit no further apart than the view kernel's half-width — 16° at max_harmonic=8.
  • That is ~22 sides for a full circle, not the "a few diverse sides" the first write-up recommended. That advice was wrong.
  • merge_tol should be derived from lobe_width(), not set by hand.
  • Widening the kernel (lower max_harmonic) buys coverage at the cost of angular resolution — it is the same trade as an SSP length scale.

Watch it turn

Press play. The left panel is the object going round; the arrows are optical flow — where each patch of the image moved between this frame and the one before. The middle panel is what the flow could not explain: bright means surface appeared or vanished there, because flow can shove pixels around but it cannot invent them. The right panel is the memory’s belief about which way it is being looked at, updating frame by frame.

The thing to watch for: the bright flashes in the middle panel are the object self-occluding — a chair back swinging past, a mug handle disappearing. The obvious guess is that those are where it goes wrong. They are not. On chair, mug or L_block, watch the error bars underneath instead: they line up with the shaded gaps — sides missing from the file — and ignore the flashes.

Then try cube, or drum. Those are red almost everywhere, and it still has nothing to do with flow: a cube looks identical from four sides, so the belief splits into competing peaks and there is no right answer to pick. That is the other failure, and it is a property of the object rather than of anything the memory did.

Measured at the corrected settings

This panel uses ssp_dim=2401, max_harmonic=4, 12 sides on file — the values FINDINGS.md §16 E2 arrives at. The sections above it use the old 151/8, which is why their degrees are larger. Flow is iterative Lucas–Kanade at radius 5, computed on the 96px render the experiments use, never on the 224px one you are looking at.

Occlusion costs 3°. The gap costs 8°.

Two things could be making the errors: the surface doing something abrupt, or simply being far from anything the memory has stored. Both were measured. It is overwhelmingly the second.

self-occlusion — barely matters

Sorting every held-out view by how much surface appeared or vanished, and comparing the smoothest quarter against the most occluded:

—

One object bucks it hard — chair, which has three times more flow than anything else, reads 16.8° at its occlusion events against 5.2° elsewhere. Across four objects, how much a thing occludes and what that costs correlate at +0.97. Four objects is a hint, not a result, and it is on the page as one.

where it breaks
  • It cannot guess sides you never looked at. Leave a 30° hole and the error inside it is ~27°.
  • A cube looks the same from four sides. That is not a mistake — there are genuinely four right answers.
  • Sharpening the code makes it worse, not better. Reach beats precision when views are sparse.

The sign and the ranking below stand — ρ is positive under every leave-one-object-out exclusion, and the aliasing split is a difference between two large groups rather than a correlation. Any interval computed by resampling frames needs a hierarchical bootstrap over objects, arcs and seeds instead.

Applying the breadth check from RESULTS_SO_FAR.md — does the effect survive removing its strongest object? — it does survive, but weakly, and the sign never flips:

The cube halves it, which is the tell: the cube has both the fastest appearance change (sharp faces flipping) and the worst error (it aliases). Rate was a proxy for symmetry, not a cause. Restricted to unimodal azimuths only, ρ falls to +0.202 and the gradient is nearly flat — median error 21.8° → 24.5° → 26.8° across the full range of appearance rate. Peak multiplicity explains the failures; appearance rate barely does.

It interpolates. It does not extrapolate.

Widening the held-out arc moves the nearest kept side further away. Error inside the gap tracks that distance almost linearly up to chance, while the control — the same object file read at sides it kept — never moves. The file is not degraded by the harder split; the missing viewpoints simply are not recoverable.

Chance is 90°. A constant predictor also scores 90°. The interleaved row is the split the earlier draft used, and it overstated accuracy by roughly 3×.

What each failure asks for

for aliasing

Break the symmetry or report the ambiguity

  • More stored sides do nothing — the peaks stay equal.
  • Return the whole likelihood, not the argmax. ViewLocalisation.margin already measures the gap to the runner-up peak, and it is small exactly here.
  • Fuse with odometry rather than trusting the peak; a flat multi-peak likelihood is still informative as a likelihood.
  • Break the tie with a cue the pooled descriptor discards — a part at a known surface location is the natural candidate.
for coverage

Store sides at the kernel's spacing

  • To localise better than 15°, sides must sit no further apart than the view kernel's half-width — 16° at max_harmonic=8.
  • That is ~22 sides for a full circle, not the "a few diverse sides" the first write-up recommended. That advice was wrong.
  • merge_tol should be derived from lobe_width(), not set by hand.
  • Widening the kernel (lower max_harmonic) buys coverage at the cost of angular resolution — it is the same trade as an SSP length scale.

Watch it turn

Press play. The left panel is the object going round; the arrows are optical flow — where each patch of the image moved between this frame and the one before. The middle panel is what the flow could not explain: bright means surface appeared or vanished there, because flow can shove pixels around but it cannot invent them. The right panel is the memory’s belief about which way it is being looked at, updating frame by frame.

The thing to watch for: the bright flashes in the middle panel are the object self-occluding — a chair back swinging past, a mug handle disappearing. The obvious guess is that those are where it goes wrong. They are not. On chair, mug or L_block, watch the error bars underneath instead: they line up with the shaded gaps — sides missing from the file — and ignore the flashes.

Then try cube, or drum. Those are red almost everywhere, and it still has nothing to do with flow: a cube looks identical from four sides, so the belief splits into competing peaks and there is no right answer to pick. That is the other failure, and it is a property of the object rather than of anything the memory did.

Measured at the corrected settings

This panel uses ssp_dim=2401, max_harmonic=4, 12 sides on file — the values FINDINGS.md §16 E2 arrives at. The sections above it use the old 151/8, which is why their degrees are larger. Flow is iterative Lucas–Kanade at radius 5, computed on the 96px render the experiments use, never on the 224px one you are looking at.

Occlusion costs 3°. The gap costs 8°.

Two things could be making the errors: the surface doing something abrupt, or simply being far from anything the memory has stored. Both were measured. It is overwhelmingly the second.

self-occlusion — barely matters

Sorting every held-out view by how much surface appeared or vanished, and comparing the smoothest quarter against the most occluded:

smoothest quarter6.5°
second8.2°
third8.5°
most occluded quarter8.8°

+2.3° across the whole range, pooled correlation +0.14. Real, and small. One object bucks it hard — chair, which has three times more flow than anything else, reads 16.8° at its occlusion events against 5.2° elsewhere. Across four objects, how much a thing occludes and what that costs correlate at +0.97. Four objects is a hint, not a result, and it is on the page as one.

distance from a stored side — matters a lot

A 30° hole has an inside. A query at its edge sits 5° from a stored side; one in the middle sits 15°. Same objects, same code:

object file a plain list of the same views

—

So the §0 E4 correction was measuring the right thing

The original evaluation held out alternate frames, which puts every single query at the 5° end of that gradient — the cheap end — and then reports it as if it were the whole arc. That is why swapping to contiguous held-out arcs roughly tripled the error. The gradient is the reason, and it is now measured rather than argued.

One setting was wrong the whole time

max_harmonic looks like a resolution knob — bigger means a sharper kernel, finer angles. It is also, and more importantly, a capacity knob: it sets how many distinct frequencies the code has, and that decides how many views you can superpose before they start interfering. Everything above this section was measured at 8. 4 is better at every number of stored sides.

median error — darker is better —

—

The winning kernel is 28° wide — wider than the descriptor’s own 22° correlation length. A broad kernel is also a low-frequency one, and low-frequency codes superpose better. §14’s “reach beats precision” and the capacity ceiling turn out to be one constraint seen from two ends.

Eight experiments, five of them wrong

Each of these was written down as a prediction with a stated way to fail, and then run. The failures did more work than the successes — E2 refuted its own hypothesis and found the setting that turned E0’s loss into a tie.

 predictedmeasured
E0 · baselinethe object file beats a list of stored views it loses — later corrected to a tie at 12× less memory
E1 · mirror stagea mirror-symmetric stage improves identification, as in face patch AL makes it worse, equally for symmetric and chiral objects
E2 · residue codea modular code holds more views per dimension it destroys capacity — but found the max_harmonic fix
E3 · scene codevectors to objects transfer across frames, as object vector cells do exactly — and motion becomes one bind
E4 · how many sidesthe descriptor’s half-width says how densely to orbit each object predicts nothing; the answer is 30° for every object
E5 · rotationrotation needs a rotation-equivariant code it can have one — but doesn’t need it
E6 · end to endthe filter smooths the viewpoint estimate it does — but its bigger job is repairing misidentification
E7 · optical flowself-occlusion is where localisation breaks costs 2.3°; the gap costs 7.8°
what came out of it
namingan unbound prototype per object, never the view book
viewpointthe view book, max_harmonic=4
sides12, one every 30°
sceneID ⊗ S(pobj − probot)
motionone bind of the whole memory
turninga 2×2 matrix on the answer, not work on the memory
symmetric objectsa first-frame hint from the scene map
the two memories fix each other

A cube looks identical from four sides and no amount of looking at it will help. But you are only standing in one of them. The scene map knows which, and it only has to know it to within 30° — half the tightest alias. One hint, at one frame:

171.8° worst-case error over a walk, appearance alone
9.4° the same walks, anchored by the scene map

Objects that are not symmetric sit at 5° either way and never needed it — which is how you know the anchor is doing what it claims and not just tightening everything.
